p: Before anybody wrote her father's name down, Consuelo had already told the 911 operator about the cap.

In her kitchen she told Dani two things no jury ever heard. The man in red was smaller than the man he hit. And at ten to eleven, by her stove clock, a little boy was out in the lot crying for his papi.
She told the young officer that night and the detective the next day, and nobody asked her again.
North of the lot, from her sink window, there's a ditch and the railroad tracks, and nowhere a truck could go.
That evening Dani found the old leaking washer on her curb, and a used one in the basement, put in and level, with one of Teo's shop rags folded on the lid.
Ana Brennan. This is the month she files.
Joel Harlan. Dani's supervisor at the public defender's office.
Luis Ruiz. At Sterling, where he teaches chess and helps men study for the GED.
Teo Ruiz. Turning thirty this month.
Lupe Ruiz. Six. She keeps asking about her grandfather.
Celia Lucero. A paralegal two desks down, who walked Dani through her first year.

Monday, March 15. Ana had printed the motion three times, on three colors of paper, so she'd know at a glance which one she had in her hand. White was the draft. Yellow was the one with her pencil all over it. The blue one was clean, and nobody had been allowed to touch it.

Dani had taken the day off. A vacation day, her own, put in on the office calendar in February under PERSONAL, which was true. She'd been up the stairs on Federal by twenty to seven with two coffees, and Ana had taken one without looking up.

Not quite thirteen weeks to June. Last Wednesday her father had moved a pawn and she'd moved a pawn. His bishop still sat on her knight's square, and neither of them had brought it up. They'd gotten good at not bringing it up.
Her list was on the whiteboard, in her own capitals from Saturday, nine lines long. Ana had looked at it all weekend, Dani guessed, and said nothing. With Ana that meant something was coming.

We file at noon, Ana said. I push a button and it goes to Brighton, and Meredith Sloane has it by lunch. We'll ask for a hearing, so the law gives her at least thirty five days to answer, and she'll use every one of them. She picked up the pencil. Between now and noon, it gets shorter.
Dicta lifted her head off the rug at the word noon, the way she did for lunch, and put it back down.
Ana's Pencil: the rule under it.
March on Federal. Somebody downstairs is running a dryer with a shoe in it, a thump every second, and Dicta has decided to sleep through it out of spite. Pencil.

Up to now you've worked one argument at a time. Somebody concluded something from something, and you asked whether it held. A principle question pulls the camera back. It asks what general rule sits under one particular decision. A coach benches a player. A city turns down a permit. A neighbor returns a borrowed ladder and apologizes for the bent rung. Which rule, if it's a good rule, makes that decision the right one?

The rule is general. The decision is about one case. Your job is to line them up. Nearly every principle has two halves, a when and a then. When a borrower damages a thing, then the borrower fixes it. Check the when against the facts: does this case actually meet it? Then check the then against the conclusion: does it say what the decision says? Both halves have to land.
The most common wrong answer has the right then and a when the facts never reach. It sounds like the case. It's about the case's cousin.

Try one. A bakery throws out the last of Tuesday's sourdough on Wednesday morning, though it looks fine, because it promises everything on its shelves was baked that day. Rule: a shop that promises bread is fresh daily shouldn't sell bread from the day before. When: the promise, and day old bread. Then: don't sell it. Both land. Now a rule that says bread should be thrown out once it goes stale. Right then. The when never happened. The loaves looked fine.

Here's where this differs from last month. When the stem asks which principle justifies the reasoning, big words don't sink you. A principle can be as sweeping as it likes. Always, every, never. If it covers this case and points at this conclusion, broad is fine. If two rules both get there, take the one that uses the argument's own reason. When the stem asks which principle the facts most strongly support, though, it works like last month: a rule that reaches far past the case is more than the facts show. What a principle can never do is sit next to the case without touching it.

How the exam asks it. These stems ask which principle, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning, or which principle the reasoning most closely conforms to, or which one the situation best illustrates. Justify questions work like a sufficient assumption: the right rule makes the conclusion follow.

Sometimes the test hands you the rule and asks you to find the case. Same work, other direction. Take the rule apart before you read a single choice. Every condition. Every unless. A rule that says a lifeguard may clear the pool when there's lightning within ten miles, unless the pool is indoors, has three pieces in it, and each wrong answer will break one of them.

One trap in particular. A rule says when something should happen. It almost never says what happens the rest of the time. If a lifeguard clears an indoor pool for lightning, the rule doesn't forbid it. It just doesn't back it. A choice that has the rule deciding a case the rule never reaches is wrong, even when the outcome sounds fair.
Some of these ask for the violation instead, or for every choice that conforms except one. Same checklist. You want the case that meets the when and does the opposite of the then.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which judgment most closely conforms to the principle, which situation it most clearly applies to, or which action violates it. List the rule's conditions in the margin first, then test each choice against the list.
Two people talk. The question asks what they disagree about. This one has the cleanest test on the whole exam, and almost nobody uses it.

Take each choice and ask both speakers. Would the first one say yes or no? Would the second? If either of them never touched it, cross it off, however much it sounds like the fight. You need one yes and one no, from what they said or plainly implied.

The second speaker almost always gives something away before attacking. Fair enough. That's true. I'll grant you that. Whatever gets conceded there is agreement, and it shows up in the choices dressed as a disagreement. Underline the concession.

Implied counts. When the second speaker answers a reason with a fact that undercuts it, you can read that speaker as rejecting the conclusion the reason was holding up. But implied means plainly implied. If you have to build three steps to get a speaker to a view, that speaker doesn't hold it.

And the fight isn't always over the first speaker's conclusion. Sometimes the second speaker goes after a reason. One says the new bridge is safe because it passed inspection. The other says the inspector only looked at the deck. They may agree the bridge is fine. What they disagree about is whether passing that inspection shows it.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask what the two speakers disagree about, or what their statements most strongly suggest they're committed to disagreeing over. Do the yes and no test on every choice, both speakers, every time.
Now and then the question flips. What do they agree on? Same test, same two speakers, and now you want two yeses. The concession you underlined is usually where it lives.

Agreement can be smaller than either side's position. One parent says the bake sale should move to the gym because rain's coming. The other says the gym's booked, so move it to the cafeteria. They fight about the room. Both are committed to one thing neither said in those words: the sale shouldn't stay out on the lawn.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which statement both speakers are committed to accepting, or which they would most likely agree with. If one speaker is silent on a choice, it's out, however reasonable it sounds.

Reading Comprehension does this too. A passage lays out a standard, a test, a set of conditions somebody uses to decide things. One question asks what principle sits under it. Another hands you a new case and asks how the passage's standard would treat it.

Same moves. Find the conditions in the passage, in the passage's own words. Run the new case through them one at a time. Don't add a condition the author never gave you because it seems sensible, and don't drop one because the case is sympathetic. The passage is the rulebook. A case it doesn't cover isn't decided by it.
When the question asks for the principle, look for the why under the conditions. The conditions are the what. Somebody picked them for a reason, and the reason is usually your answer.

Let's work one. A passage describes when a county closes a swimming beach. It closes after a water test shows bacteria over a set line, or within a day of heavy rain, which washes runoff in, and it reopens as soon as a fresh test comes back clean. A question asks for the principle underlying the policy. It isn't any one of those conditions. It's the reason they share: close a beach when there's good reason to expect the water is unsafe, and only for as long as that reason lasts. That's the general rule, put in words that would fit any case. It explains every condition and adds none.

The traps come in two sizes. Too narrow repeats one condition: beaches should close after rain. The passage does that, but it isn't the rule under all of it. Too broad sounds noble and goes too far: safety always comes before recreation, which would keep a beach shut after a clean test just in case. The variation turns the question around. It gives you the principle and asks which case conforms to the principle. Walk each case through it the way you'd walk it through a rule. A pool that shuts when a chlorine reading fails and opens when it passes conforms. A pool that shuts every Tuesday doesn't, however careful it sounds.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which case the author's standard would most likely cover, which situation is most similar, or which principle underlies a position in the passage. Point to the line that settles each choice before you pick.

Principles on this test are conditionals in a suit. A person may do this only if that, unless the other. Last month you learned to read one arrow. Tonight the rules get longer, and the trick is that a long rule is still made of the same few parts. You take it apart the same way every time, in the same order, and it stops being long.

Step one, find the result. What does the rule say happens, or may happen, or must not? With if or when in front of the conditions, the result is the back of the arrow. With only if, requires or needs, it's the other way round: the conditions go on the back and the result goes in front. Step two, find every condition and how they're joined. And means all of them. Or means any one. Step three, find the escape hatch: unless, except, without, until. That piece goes in front with a not on it. Step four, flip the whole thing, and remember the not walks inside and turns every and to or and every or to and.

Work one. A tenant may sublet only if the landlord agrees in writing and the tenant has lived there a full year. Result: sublet. Only if puts the conditions on the back. So sublet, then written consent and a full year. Both of them, because they're joined by and. Flip it: no written consent or less than a year, so no sublet. Any one missing piece is enough to stop it. Now a case. Gil has lived in the unit two years and sublet it last summer. What must be true? The landlord agreed in writing. The year doesn't settle anything, since Gil had two. The written consent is the only piece left, and the rule demands it.

Now one with the escape hatch. Unless a student has a doctor's note, a student who misses the final fails the course. Result: fails. Condition: missed the final. Escape: no note goes in front. So missed the final and no note, then fails. Flip: passed the course, so either took the final or had a note. Ruth missed the final and passed. She had a note. And what about a student with a note who missed the final? The rule goes quiet. The note gets them past this rule, and the course could still have other ways to fail.

Rules inside rules are the hardest ones on the test, and they read fine until you try to use them. If the bridge is closed, the bus may take Route 9 only if Route 9 has been plowed. The outer rule is about the bridge. Inside it is a second arrow: Route 9, then plowed. That inner arrow only switches on when the bridge is closed. So on a day the bridge is closed and the bus took Route 9, Route 9 was plowed. On a day the bridge is open, the rule has nothing to say, plowed or not. The usual trap applies the inner arrow on every day. Another trap turns it around: Route 9 was plowed, so the bus took it.

Watch for the not every and the not all. Not every volunteer gets a meal means some volunteer doesn't. It doesn't mean none do, and it doesn't tell you anyone does. Watch for neither and nor in a rule. Neither the lab nor the archive may be entered after six without a badge is two rules in one sentence: lab after six, then badge, and archive after six, then badge. And watch for each and every in the result. Every lamp in the shop is either broken or sold. To deny that, you need one lamp that's neither broken nor sold. One lamp, both failures.

Here's how it shows up in a principle question when the decision is a no. Say a tenant has written consent and has lived in the unit eight months, and the decision is that she may not sublet. The right rule makes the no follow: sublet only with consent and a full year. She fails the year, so she may not. The wrong answers come in three flavors. One names a condition the facts don't fail, sublet only with written consent, and she has it, so that rule never reaches the no. One joins the conditions with or, consent or a year, and that rule would let her sublet. And one runs the arrow backward: consent and a year are enough to sublet. That's a rule about who may, and it says nothing about a tenant who's missing a piece. On a yes decision, it turns around. If Gil may sublet because he has both, a rule that says consent and a year are enough is exactly the justify answer, and a broader or rule covers him too. Broad is fine on a justify question, the way you learned at the start of the month. So before you sort the choices, notice whether the decision says may or may not.

Three to try in your head before you look at the cards. First: no exhibit leaves the evidence room unless the clerk and the detective both sign. Exhibit 9 left. Did the detective sign? Yes, both had to. Second: the clerk signed for Exhibit 12 and the detective didn't. Did it leave? It couldn't have. Third: both signed for Exhibit 4. Did it leave? Maybe. Two signatures get it past the rule. Nobody said it went anywhere. If you got all three, the cards will go quickly. If the third one fooled you, that's the reversed arrow, and it's the one to practice.

When the stem asks you to justify a decision, check that the facts meet every condition in front of the arrow and that the result is the decision. When it asks which judgment most closely conforms to the principle, apply the principle to each specific case. Check every condition again, then make sure nobody in the choice did something the rule only allows them to do. May isn't must. A rule that says a lifeguard may clear the pool in lightning doesn't make a lifeguard who stays open break it. Breaking a may is very hard. Breaking a must not is easy. So when you apply the principle to a specific case, the judgment that most closely conforms is usually a must not that the facts trip, or a may that the facts fully earn, and almost never a must that the rule only allowed.

How the exam asks it. Principle stems with long rules are the place to slow down for ten seconds. Write result, conditions, joining word and escape hatch in the margin, then test each choice against the list. The wrong choices usually change one joining word or add one condition.
Here's a point at issue question worked through the yes and no test, because the test is only useful if you run it on every choice.

Lena says the town should move the farmers market from Saturday to Sunday, since the Saturday soccer games leave shoppers nowhere to park downtown. Ruiz answers that parking isn't the problem, because the lot behind the library sits half empty on Saturdays. What do they disagree about?

Take the choices one at a time and ask each speaker. Whether the market should move to Sunday. Lena, yes. Ruiz? He never says. He goes after her reason and stops. Maybe he'd move it for some other reason. Out, and this is the one most people pick, because it's what the fight seems to be about. Whether the soccer games are popular. Lena implies it, Ruiz never touches it. Out. Whether shoppers at the Saturday market have room to park. Lena, no. Ruiz, yes, there's room behind the library. One of each. Keep it. Whether Sunday would suit the vendors. Neither one mentions it. Out. Whether the library lot is the best place to park downtown. Neither commits to best. Out.

One survived, and it's about her reason, not her conclusion. That's the lesson from earlier tonight in action. The second speaker often attacks a premise and leaves the conclusion alone, and then the disagreement is over the premise. A choice about the conclusion sounds like the heart of it and fails the test, because one speaker never said a word about it.
How the exam asks it. Point at issue stems ask what the two speakers disagree about. Run every choice past both speakers. A choice one speaker never touched is out, however close it sounds.
Ana read her own first argument off the yellow copy, not loud, the way she'd read a grocery list.

The State took scrapings from under Travis Hensley's fingernails the morning he died. They've sat in an evidence room for nineteen years, and nobody has ever tested them. If what's under his nails belongs to a man who isn't Luis Ruiz, there's a reasonable probability no jury convicts him. So the court should order the test.

She looked up over the page. Your father says everybody was shoving in that bar. Ronnie says more. Either way there were hands in there, and Meredith will say so, and I'd rather the judge hear it from me first. That's on page six. She tapped the paragraph. A judge reads this and asks what rule I'm standing on. Which one, if it's a good rule, gets me to the test?
A. A court should order a test of old evidence once the person convicted agrees to give a sample of his own.
B. A court should order a test only when the defense can show the judge ahead of time what the result is going to be.
C. When stored evidence could point to someone else and has never been tested, a court should let it be tested.
D. Evidence that was tested before trial should be tested again whenever the methods have gotten better since.

Never tested, and it could point at somebody else. Then let them test it. That's the floor I'm standing on. Ana makes a small check in the margin. The legislature wrote close to the same thing, only longer. Something collected, never tested, and a result that could matter. It doesn't promise the result helps us. It says we get to look.

That's the one. Pencil down. Principle. My facts are that the scrapings were kept, never tested, and could belong to someone else, and my conclusion is that the court should allow the test. This rule's when matches those facts and its then matches the conclusion.
Under his nails. For a second she wasn't on Federal at all. She was fifteen in a bathroom doorway on a Sunday, and a square of tissue on her father's neck had a red dot coming through it.
If the lab ever ran those scrapings, some of what it found might be his. She'd known that since January, and she'd never said it to anybody. She didn't say it now. Ana was already holding out a page.
Before we cut anything. One sheet, typed, stapled at the corner, gone soft along the fold. I gave a talk to a room full of new lawyers in 2015. Half of them slept. This was the part I meant.

Ana Brennan, notes for a talk to new appellate lawyers, 2015. A verdict is supposed to end things. Witnesses get old and move away, evidence gets lost, and the families on both sides are owed a day when it's over. So the law doesn't reopen a verdict because somebody has found a better argument, or because a witness now sounds less sure. It reopens for evidence: something about what happened that the defense didn't have, couldn't have found with ordinary care, and that would probably have changed the verdict. That's a narrow door. It isn't narrow because judges are hostile to people in prison. It's narrow because finality is worth something too, and every exception spends some of it. If you want the door opened, be ready to say which condition your evidence meets, one at a time, without help from adjectives.
Read it like somebody else wrote it. What rule is that page standing on?
A. Judges keep the door narrow because they don't trust people in prison who come back asking for more.
B. A verdict should never be reopened once the families on both sides have been told that it's finally over and done.
C. Because finality is worth something, a verdict should reopen only for new evidence that would probably change it.
D. A lawyer who wants a verdict reopened should take the conditions one at a time and leave out the adjectives.

Finality is worth something, Dani says, so a verdict opens again only for new evidence that would probably change it. That's the page, Ana says. The rest hangs off it. The families, the door, the adjectives. She doesn't look at the line about the families. Dani does. Somewhere in Brighton it's somebody's job this week to send Shannon Hensley a letter.
Right. Now say why. Principle in a passage. The page gives a reason, finality, and the rule that comes out of it. Dani's sentence has both halves.
Ana got up and went to the whiteboard with the eraser in one hand and the pencil in the other, which Dani had never seen her do.

Dani's list, on Ana's whiteboard. 1. TEST THE SCRAPINGS. 2. BALL CAP IN THE DISPATCH LOG. PHIL HAD IT, NEVER USED IT. 3. BOY CRYING PAPI AT 10:50. TOLD TO POLICE TWICE, NEVER TURNED OVER. 4. CAP WRITTEN AND STRUCK IN GENE'S NOTEBOOK. 5. RONNIE DIDN'T SEE WHAT STARTED IT. 6. ARCHULETA, A ROOKIE, LEFT THE CAP OUT OF HIS REPORT. 7. RAN NORTH ON FOOT, NO ROAD, AWAY FROM THE TRUCKS. 8. SMALLER THAN THE VICTIM. 9. THE GUY FROM THE BAR COULD BE ANY MAN IN THE BAR

She drew a box around the first three: the scrapings, the cap in the dispatch log, the boy. She drew an arrow from Gene's struck cap up into the dispatch log cap, another from north on foot up into the same line, and one from smaller up into the boy. Then she erased Ronnie, Archuleta and the guy from the bar, one at a time, not fast.

Ronnie stays in the file. Archuleta stays in the file. The guy from the bar is an argument, and it goes where arguments go. She put the eraser down on the tray. Tell me what I just did. The rule. Not the list.
A. A point stays on the board only if there's paper behind it, not just somebody's memory of what happened that night.
B. A point stays on the board only if it's aimed at the police, not at the people who testified in 2008.
C. The points that would make a judge angriest at the State go to the top, and the others go to the bottom.
D. A point gets its own place only if, standing alone, it could change the result. The rest back one up or go.

Standing alone, Ana says. The judge could rule on the scrapings by themselves. On the cap Phil never used, by itself. On the boy. Ronnie didn't see the start? That's a reason not to lean on Ronnie. It doesn't tell anybody who was at the curb.

Good. That's how you read it. Principle. I kept the three points a court could rule on by themselves, folded the details that support them into them, and cut the ones that only weaken a witness or repeat an argument. This rule explains both the keeping and the cutting.
Dani looked at the three wiped lines. She'd sat in Ronnie's taqueria for one of them and read Archuleta's report twice on the bus for another.
They're all true, she said. Every one. Ronnie didn't see it start. Archuleta wrote down what he felt like writing down. Put them back. Each one's another reason. Nine reasons is more than three.

They're all true, Ana said. True was never the test. She sat down on the edge of the desk, which she also never did. In 2010 I filed a brief for your father with nine issues. Nine. I had a jury instruction. I had a juror who might've been asleep. I had a hearsay ruling. I had the jacket, and I put the jacket ninth. She said it to the whiteboard. The court spent ten pages on the first eight. The jacket got one sentence, on the last page, under remaining contentions. I read that sentence standing up in the hall.
Nine issues tells a judge you don't believe any of them. You're just throwing things. A breath. I knew which one it was.
She stopped there. Dicta's tags rattled once, on the rug. Whatever came after I knew, Ana kept.
Dani had read that opinion twice on the basement stairs and blamed three judges she'd never met. She'd never thought about who put the jacket ninth.
What point are Dani and Ana really at odds over?
A. "So it isn't whether they're true. We both say they are. It's whether nine makes it stronger."
B. "You think Ronnie and Archuleta lied, both of them. I think they were honest about what they saw."
C. "We're arguing over whether the judge is really going to read every page we give the court."
D. "This is about 2010, then. Whether nine was the right number for the brief you filed for him."

That's the fight, Ana says. You think reasons add up. I think they water each other down. We agree they're true. We agree about the jacket. She picks the eraser up again and doesn't use it. I've had this fight before. I lost it to myself.

That's the one. Pencil down. Point at issue. You say nine reasons beat three. My answer is my 2010 brief, where nine issues told the court I didn't believe in any of them. We've both said the points are true, which leaves the question of whether more of them makes the motion stronger.
At ten Ana handed her the blue copy, the clean one, and a pencil of her own, already sharpened.

The motion, first page, the blue copy. District Court, Adams County, Colorado. The People of the State of Colorado versus Luis Ruiz, defendant. Defendant's motion for postconviction DNA testing and for postconviction relief. Luis Ruiz, through counsel, asks the Court for two things. First, an order that the fingernail scrapings taken from Travis Hensley on October 28, 2007, which have never been tested, be tested now. Second, a new trial. The jury that convicted Mr. Ruiz in June 2008 heard that the man who struck Mr. Hensley wore a red jacket, and that Mr. Ruiz wore one that night. It did not hear that the only eyewitness told police the man also wore a ball cap, or that half an hour before the attack she heard a child crying in the lot. Then a blank line, marked in capitals: one sentence, the rule.
Your line, Ana said. The rule we're asking for, in one sentence, so a tired judge at four in the afternoon gets it. Everything after it just shows the rule fits.
A. The new evidence proves Luis Ruiz is innocent, and the court should let him out of Sterling right away.
B. A conviction should be set aside when evidence the jury never heard would probably have led it to acquit.
C. Any new evidence that raises a reasonable doubt about the verdict is enough to set the conviction aside.
D. If the defense lawyer made mistakes at trial that hurt his client, the conviction should be set aside for that.

She writes it on the blank line of the blue copy, in the pencil Ana gave her. A conviction should be set aside when evidence the jury never heard would probably have led it to acquit. Ana reads it twice, her lips moving the second time. Probably, she says. That word is the size of the standard, and you didn't let go of it. The rest we take one condition at a time.

Right. Now say why. Principle in a passage. The page sets up exactly that: what the jury didn't hear, and that it would have mattered. Probably keeps it the size of the standard. The other conditions come in when each piece has to qualify.
Ana took an index card out of her shirt pocket. She'd written it in December, Dani could tell from how soft the corners were, and she'd carried it ever since.

Ana's card. NEW. ALL FOUR. 1. The jury never heard it. 2. He and his lawyer couldn't have known it, with reasonable care. 3. It's about what happened, not only about whether somebody's believable. 4. It would probably bring an acquittal.

Everything except the DNA is late, by the calendar. More than ten years late. So for every piece we have to tell the court why it's coming in now, and the why is always the same: nobody gave it to him. That's what this card is for. She laid it on the dispatch log. Start with your cap. Run it.
A. It fails line three. A cap only goes to whether Consuelo can be believed, not to what happened out there.
B. It isn't new. Phil had the log before trial. It goes in under the claim that he should have used it.
C. It isn't new, since Phil had the log before trial. So it doesn't belong anywhere in the motion at all.
D. It's new. Nobody saw the words BALL CAP until I read the whole line in December, nineteen years later.

Line two, Ana says. Phil had it in a folder with a tab on it. Couldn't have known? He owned it. So it isn't new. It's worse than new. It's a lawyer who had the answer in his hand and highlighted the wrong half. She taps page nine. That's where it lives.

Good. That's how you read it. Application. The cap fails the second condition, because the defense had the log. That keeps it out of the new evidence claim, and it's the whole basis of the other claim, that Phil had it and didn't use it.
Now the hard one. Ana turned the card over in her fingers. The boy. Say he turns up. Grown now, whoever he is. Walks up those stairs and says he was in that lot. Run him through it.
Down on the street a bus went by, and the window shook in its frame the way it always did, and Dicta didn't wake.
A. He wouldn't count. A child that young couldn't have been a witness at any trial in the first place.
B. He'd count as long as what he says would probably have led the jury to acquit. That's the real test.
C. He'd count only if Pa and Phil couldn't have known about him in 2008, not just because we never did.
D. He'd count. Nobody has heard one word from him in nineteen years, so anything he says now is new.

New to him, Ana says. Not to us. If your father knew there was a boy out there, the boy isn't new, whatever he says. Pa didn't know about any boy. Then he might get past line two, if Phil couldn't have found him either. Ana writes it on the back of the card, small. Dani watches the pencil and doesn't think about who the boy was. She's careful about it, the way you're careful on a floor you know is wet.

That's the one. Pencil down. Application. The card's second line asks what the defendant and his lawyer could have known, so a grown witness counts as new only if they couldn't have known about him. That's the condition the case turns on.

At 11:58 Ana pressed the key, and the motion went to Brighton, and nothing happened. No sound. The screen said Submitted. Ana looked at it a while anyway. The lab, Dani said. Who pays for it? Not you, Ana said, and that was all she ever said about it.
She'd gone in at four on her day off to tell Joel herself, standing in his doorway, before he could hear it anywhere else. Tuesday, March 16, at nine, he closed his door.
The last time he'd closed it was October, and he'd said most of this then.

Same as October, Joel said. One thing more. The motion says his trial lawyer missed things. Sooner or later somebody asks whether we missed some too. When that happens the office answers, and you're not in it. Not a meeting, not a hallway, not a copy line on an email. I'm putting it in writing this afternoon. He held up a hand before she could start. Nobody thinks you'd do anything. That isn't why. If what we did in 2010 ever matters, nobody should get to ask whether his daughter was in the room.
Which rule sums up what Joel just told her?
A. "So I'm out because you don't trust me with it, and the memo is just how you say so."
B. "So anybody with a stake stays out of how the office handles it. Even somebody who'd be fair."
C. "So the office keeps its own old work out of court, no matter who it is that comes asking."
D. "So I stay out of anything about family, unless I can show you first that I'd be fair."

Even somebody who'd be fair, Joel says. Especially. The fair ones never see it coming. He writes something on a legal pad and turns it around so she can read it. It's what she said, nearly word for word. That's the memo.

Right. Now say why. Principle. Joel keeps her out because of her stake, and he says outright it isn't about whether she'd act fairly. The rule has both pieces: a stake means out, fairness doesn't change it.
At 2:40 a chat window opened in the corner of her screen. Celia Lucero, two desks down, who'd walked her through her first year in the office and still remembered how she took her coffee.

None of it in this building. That was October, in Joel's office with the door shut. And this morning, not a meeting, not a hallway.
Which reply to Celia does Joel's rule call for?
A. "Not on my login. If you look him up on yours, though, that's a different thing, I guess."
B. "Thank you. Let me ask Joel first whether that's all right, and then I'll get back to you."

She types that she can't, that Celia can't for her either, and that Ana will find him the regular way. She sends it and watches the dots. Then: ok. got it. sorry. Then, a minute later: lunch thursday? She says yes to lunch. Ana finds the officer by Friday without anybody's login.

Good. That's how you read it. Principle, apply. Joel's rule covers anything in the office done for her father, by anyone. A search in the office system on her behalf is inside it, whoever runs it. Turning it down, and saying why Celia can't either, conforms.
Wednesday, March 17, seven. Her step. The recording, and then her father, already talking.
Brennan called Monday. Legal call. They walk you down to a little room for it, with a phone on the wall.

A. "Darnell's. Nobody gave his lawyer that report, and it's about who held the knife."
B. "Benny's. That cop got fired years after the trial, so nobody could have known it then."

Darnell, her father says, and she can hear the pencil. I'll tell him. A pause. He's going to cry. He does that. Then, lower: You sound like her, you know. Brennan.

That's the one. Pencil down. Principle, apply. Darnell's report is the only one that clears the first three lines: the jury never heard it, the defense couldn't have had it, and it goes to who did it. Whether it would probably change the verdict depends on the rest of his case, but it's the only one of the four that gets that far.
Thursday a Denver news site ran four paragraphs on it. Celia sent her the link without a word, which was the kind thing.

News item, Thursday, March 18, 2027. A man serving a forty year sentence for a 2007 death outside a Commerce City bar has asked an Adams County judge for DNA testing and a new trial. Luis Ruiz, 61, was convicted in 2008 of second degree murder in the death of Travis Hensley, 31. A motion filed Monday by his lawyer, Ana Brennan, says evidence collected in 2007 was never tested. It also cites a neighbor's account, never presented at trial, that a child was heard crying in the bar's parking lot shortly before the attack. Shannon Hensley, the victim's sister, said she learned of the filing from a letter sent by the district attorney's office. "Nineteen years," she said, "and every letter I get is about him." The district attorney's office declined to comment on a pending case.
A text from Bianca. he saw the news thing. come tomorrow anyway. he wants you there. he wont say it so im saying it

Saturday, March 20. Teo was thirty. Their rental had a carport, and Bianca had strung lights under it and set up two folding tables and a space heater on an extension cord that kept tripping the kitchen breaker. Guys from the bus garage stood around the grill in their jackets. Lupe had made her father a paper crown with a three and a zero on it in glitter glue and was wearing it herself, because it fit her better.

Dani brought a box of shop rags, a hundred to the box. On top, washed and folded square, was the one he'd left on the lid of the washer. Teo looked at it a long time. That's mine. I know. You washed it. In the new washer. One corner of his mouth went up, and came back down.

It was after nine before he said anything else to her. The grill was out and the bus guys were inside watching a game, and he came and stood next to her at the edge of the carport with a beer he wasn't drinking.

You put a kid in it. Consuelo heard a boy. I didn't put him there. Nineteen years, Dani. He's got his chess guys in there. His GED guys. He's made something. Now it's in the news, with his name. And her. He tipped the bottle at the kitchen window. She's going to type his name into a phone someday and get a dead man's sister.

She asks about him, Teo. She's going to find out. Better she hears it from us. You shouldn't have done this. Ana shouldn't have filed it. It's filed because the argument's broken. Maybe it is. So what. It's going to lose, and everybody gets to read about it while it does. I don't know if it'll lose. You don't either.
What does Dani say to Teo now?
A. "Is there something about that night you're not telling me, Teo? Because I think there is."
B. "You think Pa did it, and that's why you quit going up there. That's the whole fight, Teo."
C. "You think this is going to lose. I think it's going to win. That's the whole fight, Teo."
D. "You think this shouldn't have been filed. I think it should've. That's the whole fight, Teo."

He looks at her a long time under the string lights. Yeah, he says. That's it. It doesn't fix anything. It's only the first thing all night they've both said in the same words, and they stand there with it a minute.
Right. Now say why. Point at issue. Teo: shouldn't have been filed. Dani: it's filed because the argument's broken, so yes it should. He even grants it might be broken. That's the split.

He picked the bottle back up off the hood. Turned it in his hand. Didn't drink. When he talked it was low, under the noise from the kitchen, where somebody had the game up too loud. They looked everywhere. A detective came down our basement stairs and left with Pa's jacket in a paper bag, and they never found the flashlight, and they never found anybody. Now it's some kid bawling in a parking lot, in the paper, one sentence up from Pa's name.
He looked over at the house. Through the kitchen window Lupe was up on a chair in the paper crown, and Bianca was trying to get a frosting knife away from her without starting a war about it.
I'm not having her meet him like that, he said. On somebody's phone. From some reporter she doesn't know.
What can Dani and Teo agree on?
A. "Okay. Then that part we both want, that she doesn't hear about him from a stranger on a phone."
B. "Fine. It loses, and she never has to hear about any of it. We can both live with that much."
C. "Pa never hurt anybody that night, Teo. Not one single person. You know it, and I know it."
D. "So we both think he's been in there long enough, however this ends up going with the judge in Brighton."

Yeah. He breathes out, and it hangs under the string lights for a second in the cold. From us. Inside, Lupe gives up the knife and starts bargaining for the bowl instead. Before she's seven, Dani says. He takes long enough to answer that she thinks he isn't going to. Before she's seven.
Good. That's how you read it. Point of agreement. Teo: not off a phone, not from a stranger. Dani, earlier: better she hears it from us, which rules out strangers too. Two yeses on one claim.

They did the candles at nine thirty. Thirty and one to grow on, because Lupe insisted, which set off the smoke detector, which Teo took down off the ceiling with one hand without putting down the knife. Everybody sang. Lupe sang loudest, a beat behind everybody, and made them do the last line again.

Can we tell Grandpa? she said, the crown down over one eye. That Daddy's thirty? Somebody turned the game down. Teo cut a piece of cake. Tía can tell him, he said, and put the plate in front of Dani, and that was the last thing he said to her that night.
She drove home down 104th with the heater on high and the radio off.
A text from Bianca. hes out in the truck. not because of you. he put the rags in the garage. all of them. even the one
Wednesday, March 24, seven. Her step. The new washer was running a load behind her. It was so quiet she'd come down twice that week just to check it was on.
It came Monday, her father said. Brennan's motion. I read it twice. She writes good. He moved. She moved. The bishop sat where it sat.
Lupe made him a crown, she said. For Saturday. She wanted you to know Daddy's thirty. Nothing on the line for a while. Thirty, he said.
Then, in the same voice: That part about a kid, he said. Crying in the lot. She waited. Some neighbor kid, mija. Those apartments back there were full of kids.

She'd heard that sentence before. Not from him. From Consuelo, in Consuelo's kitchen, doing the young policeman's voice: that's some kid from the apartments, ma'am. Nearly word for word, from Sterling. Maybe, she said. Yeah, he said. Tell him happy birthday. From me. Or don't. You know him.

After, she sat at the kitchen table with her notebook and the folder of copies. She was copying the dispatch log out by hand. Ana made her do that with anything that mattered, because you can't skim your own handwriting.
Her copy, by hand. Male, red jacket, ball cap, struck the victim with an unknown object.
She stopped with the pen on the O.

Unknown object. Consuelo had said something in his hand. Her young policeman had walked the ditch to the tracks with his flashlight and found nothing in anybody's hand, nothing on the ground. At trial it was something. In Ana's motion it said an object, because that was all anybody knew. All that paper, and not one page had ever given the thing a name.
She hadn't told him about any flashlight. Nobody had told anybody. There'd never been one to tell.
She picked up her phone. His name was right at the top, from Saturday. Her thumb sat on it a long time.

Then she put the phone face down on the table. Under the log line she wrote it out the way he'd said it, word for word, with the date beside it. They never found the flashlight. Teo, March 20. Her handwriting was worse than usual. She left it.
She didn't call him. She sat with her hand flat on the phone until the screen went dark on its own, and a while after that.
